title: The integumentary system
note: Skin has an epidermis of keratinized stratified squamous epithelium over a connective tissue dermis; the hypodermis lies beneath. Epidermal layers from deep to superficial: basale, spinosum, granulosum, lucidum (thick skin only), corneum. The epidermis has no blood vessels.

read.title: The life of a keratinocyte
text: The epidermis renews itself from the bottom up. In the stratum basale, a single row of stem cells sits on the basement membrane next to the dermis. When one divides, a daughter cell is pushed upward and becomes a keratinocyte.

As it rises into the stratum spinosum, the cell begins making keratin and is joined tightly to its neighbors. In the stratum granulosum it flattens and fills with keratohyalin granules, and soon its nucleus and organelles break down. In thick skin it then passes through the clear stratum lucidum. By the time it reaches the stratum corneum it is a dead, flat, keratin-filled scale, part of a waterproof surface many cells thick that is shed and replaced roughly every four weeks.

Why do the cells die? Distance is part of the answer. The epidermis has no blood vessels of its own, so its cells depend on nutrients diffusing up from capillaries in the dermis. The farther a cell travels from that supply, the less it receives.

Other cells share the epidermis. Melanocytes in the basale pass melanin to nearby keratinocytes, where it shields DNA from ultraviolet light. Merkel cells sense touch, and Langerhans cells patrol for microbes.

q.q: Why do epidermal cells die as they rise?
o: They move away from the dermal blood supply
